p.title: Understanding Partisan Cue Receptivity: Tests of Predictions from the Bounded Rationality and Expressive Utility Perspectives

ext.title: Partisan Cue Receptivity: Bounded Rationality vs Expressive Utility
ext.venue: The Journal of Politics, vol. 82, no. 3 (July 2020), pp. 1061-1077. Published online May 11, 2020.
ext.document_type: Journal article: survey experiments (five primary, two ancillary) with an individual-data meta-analysis; studies 3 and 4 were preregistered replications.
ext.coverage: Full text read: all 2,104 lines of _text\d919f3743193.txt (main text pp. 1061-1076, tables, figure notes, footnotes, discussion and references). Appendices A-I are cited but are not in the file, so appendix-only results are reported only as the main text describes them. Metadata hint corrected: full author names and journal details added from the text; the hint's author list and blank venue/DOI fields were incomplete. Annotations: one JSON file with 24 items, all of type Highlight (22 yellow, 2 green); no sticky notes or typed comments exist, so every note field is empty.
ext.research_question: Why do citizens follow partisan cues when forming policy judgments? Is cue receptivity strongest among people with low cognitive resources (bounded rationality, cue-taking as effort-saving), or among people with both strong partisan social identity and high cognitive resources (expressive utility, effortful identity-protective reasoning)?
ext.theory: Bounded rationality (Simon 1972; Kam 2005; Lupia and McCubbins 1998): cues are heuristics that let low-resource citizens adopt value-consistent positions without costly effort, so cue receptivity should be highest among those low in cognitive resources. Expressive utility (Kahan 2013; Petersen et al. 2013; Lodge and Taber 2013; Groenendyk 2013): cue-following is identity-protective motivated reasoning, so the strongest cue receptivity should appear among people with strong partisan social identity who also have the resources to rationalize the party position. The authors treat the strong-identity-by-high-resource interaction as the key distinctive prediction of expressive utility (p. 1063).
ext.data: Study 1 (food irradiation): Survey Sampling International panel, July 2016; 883 respondents, 747 analyzed (136 excluded for no party ID or leaning). Study 2 (farm subsidy): Qualtrics panel, June 2017; 1,302 partisans in text (647 Democrats, 655 Republicans), but Table 3 reports N = 1,258; discrepancy not explained in main text. Study 3 (replication of studies 1 and 2): Bovitz Forthright sample, October 2018, N = 1,911 (appendix C). Study 4 (replication of food irradiation): Amazon MTurk, October 2018, N = 2,509 (appendix D). Individual-data meta-analysis of studies 1-4 (Table 4): 8,116 observations in CRT models, 5,607 in NfC and latent-resource models. Ancillary: US trade policy experiment (July 2016) and Danish ideology experiment (August 2017), both without a no-cues control (appendices H and I). Unit: individual respondent who identifies with or leans toward a party (the Danish study uses ideological identity). Outcome: policy support on a 0-1 scale (study 2 uses a seven-point item rescaled 0-1). Fieldwork 2016-2018.
ext.method: OLS regression of policy support on in-party and out-party cue dummies (control is omitted category), partisan social identity strength (PSID), one cognitive resource measure, and covariates (gender, age, education, race, party). The bounded rationality test uses cue-by-resource and cue-by-PSID two-way interactions. The expressive utility test uses cue x PSID x resource three-way interactions, plotted as marginal effects at -1 SD, mean, and +1 SD of PSID and resources. Individual-data meta-analysis (studies 1-4, and separately seven experiments for the in-party vs out-party contrast) uses mixed-effects regression with dummies for studies and random intercepts for study and individual. Studies 3 and 4 also measured depth of processing (reading time, thought-listing word count, factual quiz) to test the proposed mechanism.
ext.identification: Random assignment to cue condition (in-party cue, out-party cue, or control; ancillary studies compare in-party vs out-party only) identifies the cue main effects. Cognitive resources and PSID are pretreatment measures, not manipulated, so the moderation tests are observational interactions. The authors state they cannot identify causal effects of cognitive resources on cue-following (p. 1075). The key tests are three-way interactions, which are individually often nonsignificant. Analyses are OLS with covariates; replication files also run models without covariates (fn. 9).
ext.scope: US partisans (identifying with or leaning toward a major party) in four online panels (SSI, Qualtrics, Bovitz Forthright, MTurk) fielded 2016-2018. Issues were chosen to be not yet strongly partisan (food irradiation ban; farm subsidies), so findings are about cue-following on newly politicized issues (pp. 1073-1074). Panels are non-probability and the paper does not report their representativeness in the main text. Ancillary Denmark study covers ideology rather than party. Institutional scope: one-shot embedded survey experiments, not repeated elite messaging or real information environments (p. 1076).

key_findings.finding: No support for the bounded rationality prediction. Cue effects are not stronger among low cognitive resource respondents, and in several cases the interaction points the opposite way.
key_findings.location: Abstract p. 1061; study 1 p. 1065; study 2 p. 1066; meta-analysis p. 1070
key_findings.numbers: Study 1: none of six cue x resource interactions significant; in 5 of 6 the sign is opposite to the BR prediction. Study 2: all eight cue x resource interactions opposite to BR; seven nonsignificant, one significant (political knowledge x out-party cue).

key_findings.finding: Study 1 main effects: out-party cue reduces support; in-party cue effect not significant.
key_findings.numbers: Out-party cue -0.06 points on 0-1 scale (p < .01); in-party cue +0.03 (not significant). N = 747.

key_findings.finding: Study 1, expressive utility (NfC): among high need-for-cognition respondents, the in-party cue effect grows with partisan identity strength; the three-way term is significant for in-party cue only. CRT and latent-resource three-way terms are not significant.
key_findings.location: Study 1, p. 1065-1066; Table 2 model 4; Figure 1 middle row
key_findings.numbers: In-party x NfC x PSID b = 1.08 (SE .49, p = .027). Simple slope of in-party cue on PSID among high NfC b = .26 (SE .11, p = .019). Out-party analogue b = -.14 (SE .11), not significant. Out-party three-way b = -.53 (SE .51).

key_findings.finding: Study 2, expressive utility: out-party cue effect is larger for strongly identified partisans among high-CRT respondents; political knowledge gives a similar out-party pattern; NfC and latent-resource terms point the expected way but are not significant.
key_findings.numbers: CRT: out-party x PSID x CRT b = -.78 (SE .34, p = .02); in-party three-way b = .29 (SE .37), not significant. Among high-CRT respondents, strong identifiers were more influenced by out-party cues than weak identifiers, b = -.27 (SE .12, p = .02); no parallel for in-party cue. Political knowledge: out-party three-way b = -.68 (SE .28, p = .02); in-party b = .54 (SE .28, p = .05, nearly significant).

key_findings.finding: Study 2 main effects: out-party cue reduces support; in-party cue has no effect.
key_findings.numbers: Out-party cue -0.07 on 0-1 scale; in-party cue no significant influence. N = 1,302 in text (Table 3 note reports N = 1,258).

key_findings.finding: Replications (study 3, Bovitz Forthright, and study 4, MTurk) do not support the expressive utility or bounded rationality model in the same way as studies 1 and 2. Study 3 shows again no BR support and mixed EU support; study 4 shows no support for either model.
key_findings.location: Pp. 1069; appendices C.1-C.2 (study 3) and D.1-D.5 (study 4); discussion pp. 1073-1074; fn. 18 p. 1076
key_findings.numbers: Study 3 N = 1,911; study 4 N = 2,509 (Table 1). Study 4 showed no trace of the patterns in other studies; its CRT means were significantly higher than study 3 (app. D.5).

key_findings.finding: Proposed mechanism not supported: strongly identified, high-resource partisans did not process policy information more deeply on reading time, thought listing, or factual quiz measures.
key_findings.location: Pp. 1069-1070 (preregistered prediction); appendices C.3-C.5 (study 3) and D.3 (study 4); discussion pp. 1073-1074
key_findings.numbers: Null results across all depth-of-processing measures in studies 3 and 4 (the paper reports no coefficients in the main text). Exploratory reading-time ranking (after Petersen et al. 2013) also found no evidence (fn. 11).

key_findings.finding: Meta-analysis of studies 1-4: out-party cue lowers support, in-party cue raises it, and cue effects are not larger among low-resource respondents. Three-way terms are in the expressive utility direction, but only two reach significance.
key_findings.numbers: Out-party cue -0.07 points; in-party cue +0.03 points (app. E.2). In-party x PSID x NfC b = .45 (SE .17); in-party x PSID x latent resources b = .50 (SE .20); in-party x PSID x CRT b = .09 (SE .10), not significant. Out-party three-way terms negative but not significant (CRT -.11, NfC -.10, latent -.17).

key_findings.finding: Meta-analysis slopes among high-resource respondents: the in-party cue effect increases with partisan identity strength. Substantively, for latent resources the effect rises about 15 percentage points from lowest to highest PSID among high-resource respondents.
key_findings.numbers: Among high resources, in-party cue x PSID slope: CRT b = .09 (SE .04, p < .05); NfC b = .15 (SE .05, p < .01); latent b = .15 (SE .05, p < .01). Out-party x PSID slope among high CRT b = -.09 (SE .05, p < .05).

key_findings.finding: Ancillary in-versus-out-party meta-analysis (seven experiments, including trade policy and Danish ideology): no evidence cue receptivity is stronger among low-resource people; the in-party vs out-party x resource x PSID interactions are all positive; NfC and latent-resource terms are significant, CRT is not.
key_findings.location: Pp. 1071 and 1072-1073 (Table 4 continued); appendix E.3 for full analysis; apps. H and I for ancillary studies
key_findings.numbers: NfC three-way b = .55 (SE .16); latent resources b = .56 (SE .17); CRT b = .11 (SE .08), not significant. Study 3 food and study 4 MTurk coefficients listed in Table 4 are the study-level dummies.

key_findings.finding: Issue dependence: in-party cue patterns are stronger in the food irradiation (change) studies, out-party cue patterns are stronger in the farm subsidy (status quo) studies. The authors offer this as a speculative explanation.
key_findings.numbers: Qualitative; no coefficients given in the text for this contrast beyond the reported study results.

key_findings.finding: Overall conclusion: the evidence is inconsistent with bounded rationality and only partially consistent with expressive utility, so identity-expressive motives more often account for cue-following than compensation for low cognitive resources.
key_findings.numbers: Authors state the three-way interactions usually did not reach significance individually; in the second meta-analysis, three-way interactions were significant in line with EU in two of three cases (p. 1075).

limitations: Experimental stimuli cover only a small fraction of political messages; variation in issue type, framing and wording may change both the extent and motives of cue-following (p. 1074). Salient, politicized issues may mute effects (p. 1074).

Results depend on the cognitive resource measure: NfC and latent resources support EU more than the CRT, and CRT was consistent with the BR-null finding as well (p. 1075; fn. 8 on 3-item vs 7-item CRT in study 2).
Cognitive resources were not manipulated, so no causal claim about their effect on cue-following. Resources may proxy careful reading or another motivation to toe the party line (p. 1075).
Depth-of-processing mechanism was not supported; the measures (reading time, thought listing, quiz) may not capture rationalization effort (p. 1074). Authors say the mechanism remains untested.
Individual three-way interactions usually did not reach conventional significance; only two of six meta-analytic three-way effects were significant (p. 1075).
Study 4 (MTurk) produced no patterns; the authors suggest platform effects (higher CRT means, possible CRT overuse), and note MTurk may not be ideal for such studies (fn. 18, p. 1076).

One-shot manipulations embedded in attitude surveys do not replicate the repeated, cacophonous political information environment; the paper speaks to short-term cue-following on newly politicized issues, not stable attitudes (p. 1076).
Issues were chosen to be not yet strongly partisan, which limits generalization to already polarized issues (p. 1073).
Two ancillary studies lack a no-cues condition and cannot speak to presence vs absence of cues; the Danish study uses ideological rather than partisan identity (fn. 15).

The paper's explanation of issue-dependence (in-party vs out-party strength) is post hoc and speculative; sampling, method, and political environment differences across studies are not ruled out (p. 1074).
Speculation that elite polarization could be self-reinforcing through identity-driven conformity among reflective partisans is not tested here (p. 1076).
Panels are online, non-probability samples; representativeness is not reported in the main text. Study 2 N in text (1,302) differs from Table 3 (1,258).
measures: Partisan social identity strength: 8-item scale (Bankert, Huddy and Rosema 2017), averaged and rescaled 0-1; example item 'When I speak about the [party] I usually say we instead of they'. Asked of those identifying with or leaning to a party (pp. 1063-1064).

Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT): 3 items in study 1; 7 items (Toplak, West and Stanovich 2014) in studies 2 and 3; 7-item scale combining CRT-2 (4 items) and 3 CRT-7 items in study 4. Scored as proportion correct (pp. 1064-1065).
Need for cognition (NfC): 18-item scale (Cacioppo, Petty and Kao 1984) in studies 1 and 2; 10-item scale (Bakker and Lelkes 2018) in study 3; 0-1 rescaled. Not measured in study 4 (p. 1065).
Political knowledge: 10 multiple-choice items (ANES-style; Clifford and Jerit 2016) in study 2 only, proportion correct (p. 1065).
Latent cognitive resources: factor scores from a confirmatory factor analysis of all CRT, NfC and (study 2) knowledge items, rescaled 0-1; studies 1-3 (p. 1065).
Depth of processing (studies 3 and 4): reading time for the policy description; word count of thoughts listed after reading; factual quiz (four items food irradiation, two items farm) (p. 1068-1069).
Policy support: food irradiation on a 0-1 scale; farm subsidy on a seven-point item rescaled 0-1 (study 2, M = .71, SD = .25) (pp. 1063, 1066).
Covariates: gender, age (years), education (three levels), race (white vs nonwhite), party (Democrat vs Republican) (p. 1064).
references_of_note: Lenz, Gabriel S. 2013. Follow the Leader? (voters respond to politicians' policies; relevant to elections, cited for issue becoming partisan through messaging)

Huddy, Mason and Aare 2015, APSR: expressive partisanship, campaign involvement, political emotion (paper says cognitive resources and PSID are associated with political activism; relevant to elections/mobilization)
Layman and Carsey 2002, Political Behavior: party polarization and structuring of policy attitudes (elite-driven attitude sorting)
Abramowitz 2010, The Disappearing Center: engaged citizens and polarization (paper cites it for elite polarization and party-line positions among engaged citizens)
Lupia and McCubbins 1998, The Democratic Dilemma: basis for the bounded rationality/cue-taking argument
Kam 2005, Political Behavior: cue-taking and individual differences (main BR prior evidence)
Bullock 2011, APSR: elite influence on public opinion in an informed electorate (cue effect size benchmark)
Nicholson 2012, AJPS: polarizing cues (partisan cue effects)
Arceneaux and Vander Wielen 2017, Taming Intuition: need for affect and NfC interplay with partisan cues
Groenendyk 2013, Competing Motives in the Partisan Mind: directional motive plus accuracy motive; high-resource partisans stick with party
Kahan 2013, Judgment and Decision Making: expressive utility/motivated reasoning and CRT
Petersen et al. 2013, Political Behavior: party cues increase processing effort (basis of EU depth-of-processing prediction)
Lodge and Taber 2013, The Rationalizing Voter: motivated reasoning among partisans
Bakker and Lelkes 2018, Journal of Politics: abbreviated NfC measure used in study 3
Bankert, Huddy and Rosema 2017, Political Behavior: partisan social identity strength measure
Lavine, Johnston and Steenbergen 2012, The Ambivalent Partisan; Levendusky 2009, The Partisan Sort; McCarty, Poole and Rosenthal 2006 (elite polarization context)
Note: the paper contains no network, lobbying, path-finding, or allocation content; elections relevance is limited to activism, elite polarization and voter responsiveness claims.

rel.summary_md:
Bakker, Lelkes and Malka ran four US survey experiments, plus two ancillary ones and a pooled individual-data meta-analysis, on partisans in online panels from 2016 to 2018. The issues (food irradiation and farm subsidies) were chosen because they were not yet partisan. The paper tests two accounts of why people follow party cues. Bounded rationality says low-resource citizens use cues to save effort. Expressive utility says strong identifiers with high cognitive resources use cues to protect their party identity.

Bounded rationality gets no support. Cue effects are no larger among low-CRT, low-NfC or low-knowledge respondents, and most interaction signs run the other way. Expressive utility gets partial support. In the meta-analysis, among high-resource respondents the in-party cue effect rises with partisan identity strength (slope .15 for NfC and latent resources), about 15 points from the weakest to the strongest identifiers. Only two of six three-way terms are significant, and the MTurk replication shows nothing.

The finding that matters most for Melange is the main-effect asymmetry. The out-party cue reduces support by .06 to .07 on a 0-1 scale, which is a significant repulsion. The in-party cue adds only about +.03 and is non-significant in studies 1 and 2. The engine cites this paper (paired with Furnas) for `cpf_pressure`, which scores co-partisan pressure at x1.7 and out-partisan pressure at a positive x0.5. The paper shows something different: out-party cues push the receiver away, and in-party cues are weak.

The subjects are members of the public reading one-shot survey vignettes, not legislators pressing other legislators. The evidence is therefore a direction-of-sign check for the engine, not a source for its constants.

bearings.paper_claim: Out-party cues lower policy support: -0.06 (study 1, p<.01, N=747), -0.07 (study 2), and -0.07 in the pooled meta-analysis of studies 1-4. In-party cues add +0.03, non-significant in studies 1 and 2 and +0.03 pooled. The out-party effect is negative and larger in magnitude than the in-party effect, so no positive co-/out-partisan persuasion ratio exists to calibrate. The component's question, whether the ratio is near 1.7/0.5 = 3.4, is answered no: the out-party sign is reversed.
bearings.paper_location: Study 1 p.1065; study 2 p.1066; meta-analysis pp.1070-1071, Table 4, app. E.2
bearings.system_side: cpf_pressure returns 1.7 for co-partisans, 0.5 for out-partisans and 1.0 otherwise. The docstring labels this 'Furnas/Bakker source-alignment'. flip_model sums PRO neighbours into nA and ANTI neighbours into nB, both weighted by cpf_pressure, so an out-party pro-CU neighbour still adds positive pull at half weight. The dashboard align() mirrors this with K.SRCPRO/K.SRCANTI.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The sign result transfers only as a direction check. The paper measures mass-public respondents' 0-1 support for low-salience policies after one cue embedded in a survey, from 2016 to 2018 online non-probability panels. It does not measure legislator-to-legislator pressure, cosponsorship, or repeated lobbying. Two numbers do not transfer: the 1.7 amplification (the paper's in-party effect is small and often null) and any positive out-party weight (the paper finds repulsion). Elite-level cue evidence, such as Box-Steffensmeier et al. on Dear Colleague letters, would be needed to set legislator-side constants.

bearings.paper_claim: Out-party cues repel: about -0.07 on a 0-1 scale, pooled across studies 1-4. That is backfire, not a null. Heterogeneity in cue-following runs through partisan identity strength combined with cognitive resources (NfC, latent resources), not through any bipartisan-bridge attribute. The authors also note that real messages usually carry both in-party and out-party cues (p.1074).
bearings.system_side: BAKKER_XCUE is on by default. Cross-party pro-cues in the priming pressure and recruit terms are multiplied by sqrt(bpf_u*bpf_v) and clamped at 0. Perfect bridge pairs keep full positive influence, and non-bridge out-party cues fall to about 0. The comment calls the paper 'null-to-backfire'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports clamping out-party cues at 0 or below as a conservative direction. The clamp still understates the paper, which finds a negative effect. Two parts of the design have no support in the paper: the bridge exemption (sqrt(bpf) restoring full positive cross-party influence) and the bpf gate itself, because the paper never measures bipartisanship. The scope is mass public on new issues, so even the sign is an analogy for elite cosponsorship recruitment.

bearings.paper_claim: Out-party cues push partisans away from the cued position (-0.06 to -0.07), and in-party cues pull weakly (+0.03). The authors speculate that the effects depend on the issue: out-party patterns were stronger on the status-quo farm-subsidy issue, and in-party patterns were stronger on the change issue, food irradiation.
bearings.system_side: The retreat regime moves co-partisans +1 and out-partisans -1. The rally regime moves co-partisans +1 and moves out-partisans +0.5 only when bpf >= 0.30. The dashboard execMode 'oppose' amplifies counter-mobilization and is attributed in the brain to Bakker and Furnas.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The out-partisan repulsion in retreat and backfire matches the paper's out-party sign at the mass level. The paper shows no positive out-party movement, so it does not support the rally regime's +0.5 out-partisan step; that step rests on Noble & Turner alone. The issue-dependence finding is post hoc and should not be used to choose a regime.

bearings.paper_claim: Cue receptivity is not higher among low-resource people. Among high-resource respondents, the in-party cue effect rises with partisan identity strength (meta slopes: NfC b=.15, latent b=.15, CRT b=.09), about 15 points from the lowest to the highest identity strength. Strong, reflective identifiers conform most.
bearings.system_side: Behavioural susceptibility is .40 cooperation_v2 + .30 N - .20 diligence - .10 dominance, an effort-dampening prior that the module's own docstring calls a design prior, not a Byrne finding. The layer has no partisan-identity-strength term. Cooperation_v2, a cross-party share, raises susceptibility.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This bearing is weak. The paper studies the mass public, and legislators are nearly uniformly high-resource and strongly identified, so the moderator has little range in Congress. The paper's point is that conformity to party cues is identity-driven, not a by-product of low effort. That fits poorly with a design prior in which diligent members resist pressure, but the paper concerns party cues, not lobbying pressure. This is UNVERIFIED agent analysis (DE-062).

gaps_exposed: No component has a negative out-party cue term. cpf_pressure keeps out-party pressure positive (x0.5), and lt_priming clamps at 0. The paper's central main effect is out-party repulsion of about -0.07.
The 1.7 and 0.5 constants are uncalibrated. The paper's in-party effect (+0.03, often non-significant) gives no basis for amplifying co-partisan pressure, yet the code cites Bakker for it.
The only identity variable in the engine is bpf, a cosponsorship bridging share. It is not a measure of partisan identity strength, which is the moderator the paper actually finds.

No elite-level cue calibration exists. The kernel's partisan constants rest on mass-public survey experiments; an elite cue-taking study such as Box-Steffensmeier et al. on Dear Colleague letters would transfer more directly.
flags: Citation over-claim: moneyball_core.py:11 and tpl:585 attribute 'co-partisan x1.7 / out x0.5' persuasion to Furnas/Bakker. Bakker shows out-party cues as negative, not attenuated-positive, so the Bakker half of the citation does not support a positive 0.5.

lt_priming.py:57 describes the paper as 'null-to-backfire'. The pooled out-party effect (-0.07) is a significant backfire. The brain's run-4j forward item asked to 'sign out-party cues <=0 (backfire, not mere attenuation)'. The live clamp at 0, combined with the bridge exemption, carries that out only partly.
The bridge exemption in lt_priming (sqrt(bpf) restores full cross-party influence) is credited to Bakker, but the paper measures no bipartisanship or bridging attribute.
Every bearing here is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's position cites Bakker (highlighted) under cascade-kernel ('source identity and party as filters on receptiveness') and under lt-priming. His highlights stress three things: no support for bounded rationality, mixed support for expressive utility, and the remark that real messages carry both in-party and out-party cues. The paper agrees that party filters receptiveness. It disagrees on how. The filter mainly repels out-party cues and only weakly amplifies in-party cues, so the system's x1.7 co-partisan and positive x0.5 out-partisan weights do not follow from it. His highlight on elite polarization reinforcing itself among reflective partisans has no counterpart in the system. His note is not stale. The system took the paper up only partly: lt_priming signing is live, but cpf_pressure and flip_model still treat out-party pressure as positive.

related.why: The code cites the two papers together as 'Furnas/Bakker source-alignment' for cpf_pressure. Furnas covers who delivers the ask, and Bakker covers the sign of party cues; they need to be separated when the constants are justified.
Observational counterpart: elite party cues and out-party backlash in news coverage of climate. It is consistent with Bakker's out-party repulsion, and Paul highlighted it beside Bakker.
An elite cue-taking study set inside Congress (Dear Colleague letters). It is a closer analogue for legislator-side constants than Bakker's mass-public experiments.
Supplies the co- and out-partisan asymmetric response used in salience_shock. Bakker's mass-level out-party repulsion supports the retreat and backfire signs but not the rally out-partisan +0.5 step.
